blocks.text: Data collection is gathering relevant information for a purpose. Surveys, observations and experiments each have their own strengths; the right method depends on the research objective and the type of data needed.

blocks.alt: Top left: dot plots of Class A scores 50 to 60 and Class B scores 30 to 90 with mean lines and shaded one-standard-deviation bands. Top right: three boxes for survey, observation and experiment with examples. Bottom: a grade table with the misspelt name Alie and a missing grade for Sara, an arrow, and the cleaned table with Ali and 75, plus notes on imputation, flagging and removal.
blocks.caption: Spread of data, collection methods and data cleaning (original diagram after topics 5.2 and 5.3).
blocks.long_description: Class A's five scores sit close together around a mean of 54.8, with standard deviation 3.54, while Class B's scores spread from 30 to 90 around a mean of 59, with standard deviation 21.31, so the same average can hide very different spreads. Data can be collected by surveys that ask set questions, observations that watch without interfering, or experiments that change one variable. Cleaning corrects the misspelt name Alie to Ali and fills Sara's missing grade, here with 75; a missing value can also be imputed from an average, flagged, or left out of an analysis.
